title: Amaterasu: Light and Withdrawal
subtitle: An offense, a cave, and a staged return

learningObjectives.text: What does Susanoo do to Amaterasu?
How is the sun brought back?

offense.work: Old-World Japan: Old-World Japan, Susa-no-o's actions before Amaterasu withdraws
offense.author: Frank Rinder
offense.locator: Old-World Japan, Susa-no-o's actions before Amaterasu withdraws; local text normalized characters 14365-15621
offense.excerpt: Susa-no-o, the brother of Ama-terasu, who had resigned his ocean sceptre and now reigned as the Moon-God, was jealous of his sister's glory and world-wide sway. The Heaven-Illuminating Spirit had but to whisper and she was heard throughout her kingdom, even in the depths of the clear pool and in the heart of the crystal. Her rice-fields, whether situated on hill-side, in sheltered valley, or by running stream, yielded abundant harvests, and her groves were laden with fruit. But the voice of Susa-no-o was not so clear, his smile was not so radiant. The undulating fields which lay around his palace were now flooded, now parched, and his rice crops were often destroyed. The wrath and jealousy of the Moon-God knew no bounds, yet Ama-terasu was infinitely patient and forgave him many things. Once, as was her wont, the Sun-Goddess sat in the central court of her glorious home. She plied her shuttle. Celestial weaving maidens surrounded a fountain whose waters were fragrant with the heavenly lotus-bloom: they sang softly of the clouds and the wind and the lift of the sky. Suddenly, the body of a piebald horse fell through the vast dome at their feet: the "Beloved of the Gods" had been "flayed with a backward flaying" by the envious Susa-no-o.
offense.note: Rinder's modern retelling, not a direct Kojiki translation.

cave.work: Old-World Japan: Old-World Japan, the Heavenly Rock Dwelling
cave.author: Frank Rinder
cave.locator: Old-World Japan, the Heavenly Rock Dwelling; local text normalized characters 15621-15888
cave.excerpt: Ama-terasu, trembling at the horrible sight, pricked her finger with the weaving shuttle, and, profoundly indignant at the cruelty of her brother, withdrew into a cave and closed behind her the door of the Heavenly Rock Dwelling. The universe was plunged in darkness.
cave.note: Rinder's modern retelling, not a direct Kojiki translation.

festival.work: Old-World Japan: Old-World Japan, Uzume's dance and Amaterasu's return
festival.author: Frank Rinder
festival.locator: Old-World Japan, Uzume's dance and Amaterasu's return; local text normalized characters 17525-19114
festival.excerpt: The great festival began. Uzume, the goddess of mirth, led the dance and song. Leaves of the spindle tree crowned her head; club-moss, from the heavenly mount Kagu, formed her sash; her flowing sleeves were bound with the creeper-vine; and in her hand she carried leaves of the wild bamboo and waved a wand of sun-grass hung with tiny melodious bells. Uzume blew on a bamboo flute, while the eight hundred myriad deities accompanied her on wooden clappers and instruments formed of bow-strings, across which were rapidly drawn stalks of reed and grass. Great fires were lighted around the cave, and, as these were reflected in the face of the mirror, "the long-singing birds of eternal night" began to crow as if the day dawned. The merriment increased. The dance grew wilder and wilder, and the gods laughed until the heavens shook as if with thunder. Ama-terasu, in her quiet retreat, heard, unmoved, the crowing of the cocks and the sounds of music and dancing, but when the heavens shook with the laughter of the gods, she peeped from her cave and said: "What means this? I thought heaven and earth were dark, but now there is light. Uzume dances and all the gods laugh." Uzume answered: "It is true that I dance and that the gods laugh, because in our midst is a goddess whose splendour equals your own. Behold!" Ama-terasu gazed into the mirror, and wondered greatly when she saw therein a goddess of exceeding beauty. She stepped from her cave and forthwith a cord of rice-straw was drawn across the entrance. Darkness fled from the Central Land of Reed-Plains, and there was light.
festival.note: Rinder's modern retelling, not a direct Kojiki translation.

narrativeBlocks.title: The storm god's rampage
narrativeBlocks.body: Susanoo, ordered to rule the sea, instead storms up to his sister Amaterasu's realm: he wrecks her rice paddies, fouls her hall, and in the worst outrage takes a heavenly piebald horse and, flaying it with a backward flaying, hurls its carcass through her weaving-hall roof.

narrativeBlocks.title: The sun shuts herself away
narrativeBlocks.body: A weaving-maiden is struck dead; Amaterasu, appalled, retreats into the Heavenly Rock Dwelling and seals it with a boulder. The world goes dark — and in the darkness all manner of calamity stirs.

narrativeBlocks.title: The noisiest plan ever hatched
narrativeBlocks.body: Eight hundred myriads of gods gather at the cave mouth. Their plan is not force but theatre: they hang a mirror and jewels in a tree, roosters crow, and the goddess Uzume dances a wild, scandalous dance — the gods roar with laughter.

narrativeBlocks.title: Curiosity opens the door
narrativeBlocks.body: Amaterasu peeks out: what could be funnier than her light? The mirror shows her own radiance — and while she stares, a god pulls her out and a sacred rope seals the cave behind her. Light returns to the world.

narrativeBlocks.title: A festival that worked
narrativeBlocks.body: This is why Japanese matsuri are noisy and communal: the myth says the way back from darkness is shared joy, not power. The gods' racket is the world's first festival.

quiz.prompt: Why does the world go dark?

choices.text: The storm god devours the sun
Amaterasu hides in the Heavenly Rock Dwelling after Susanoo's outrages — the sun itself withdraws
The moon blocks the sun in vengeance

quiz.explanation: The darkness is her grief and shock — not an attack on the sun but its withdrawal.

quiz.prompt: How do the gods bring her back?

choices.text: Uzume's wild dance makes the gods laugh; Amaterasu's curiosity — and her own reflection — draws her out
They bribe her with new lands

quiz.explanation: The sun returns through laughter and curiosity — the world's first festival.
